clue.text: Produce I bake in churns — it's an uphill thing

parts.note: to mount a play or show is to produce it

indicators.note: to churn is to stir violently, so the letters are turned over into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A farm producer churning butter while baking, then admitting the whole job is an uphill struggle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Produce' looks like a noun for farm goods, but it is the verb, as in mounting a production; 'churns' sounds like dairy work and is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A bicycle built with gears and sturdy tyres for climbing rough hills and trails is literally a machine for going uphill.

clue.text: Pairing's gripping tango that goes across the floor

indicators.note: something gripping another holds it tightly, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: mating is the pairing of animals
Tango is T in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A dance couple locked in a tango as they sweep across the ballroom floor.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures dancers crossing the floor, but the definition is a floor covering. Tango as T comes from the NATO phonetic alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Matting is a coarse woven covering laid down over a floor surface, so it literally spans the boards underfoot.

clue.text: Posh shirt, say, I teamed with article that's perfect

parts.note: U means upper-class, as in 'U and non-U' usage
a shirt is an example of a top; 'say' flags the example
taken as written
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Someone smugly pairing an expensive shirt with a newspaper article they consider flawless.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from the 1950s debate about 'U and non-U' English, and is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopia is an imagined ideal society, so anything utopian is idealised and flawless, though often unrealistically so.

clue.text: Time vortex on display in Paddington?

definitions.note: Paddington is an example of the answer, flagged by the question mark

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
an eddy is a small whirlpool or vortex
to bear a mark or sign is to display it

explanation.surface: A sci-fi time vortex exhibited at Paddington, the London railway station.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddington sounds like the London station, but it is the bear of the children's books. In a down clue, 'on' puts the first pieces above the last one.
explanation.definitionFit: Paddington Bear, the duffel-coated character from Peru, is a famous stuffed toy bear, so he is one instance of the type.

clue.text: Granny breaking that is silly

indicators.note: breaking into something means entering it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: i.e. stands for id est, 'that is'
nan is a familiar word for a grandmother

explanation.surface: A grandmother crashing through something, which strikes the onlooker as ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that is' looks like a link phrase, but 'that' gives the IE that NAN breaks into, and only 'is' joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane describes remarks or behaviour lacking sense or substance, a close synonym for foolish or empty-headed.

clue.text: Lobbyists putting out BT broadcast in high-handed style

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters things widely, so the remaining letters are strewn into a new order
to put something out is to eject it, so those letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: Lobbyists getting a message out on British Telecom networks, in an overbearing manner.
explanation.walkthrough: BT looks like the phone company, but it is just two letters removed from the first word, leaving LOBYISS to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting bossily means giving orders in a domineering, overbearing way, which is what high-handed conduct is.

clue.text: A row over filling kiosk's walls with English amateur's notes

indicators.note: to fill something is to occupy its interior, so this goes inside
the walls of a building are its outer edges, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something over flips its order end to end

parts.note: an oar is what you row with
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An argument breaks out at a kiosk whose walls are plastered with an English hobbyist's scribbled notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' reads as a quarrel but is rowing a boat, giving OAR. A plus the turned OAR sits between the K's, then E follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Karaoke is singing along to backing tracks, usually by untrained enthusiasts, so the notes produced are those of amateur performers.

clue.text: Threatening to mutiny aboard submarine, make speech interrupted by pandemonium

indicators.note: something interrupted has another thing break into its middle

parts.note: aboard a vessel is in it
sub is the short form of submarine
to orate is to make a speech
a din is a loud chaotic noise

explanation.surface: A crew member on a submarine rabble-rousing about mutiny while chaos erupts around them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make speech' is a single idea, with 'make' just a joining word; the noise of pandemonium then breaks into the speech verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Insubordinate means defiant of authority and refusing orders, the mood of sailors on the verge of mutiny.

clue.text: India's out for long-suffering European wearing foam shoe material

indicators.note: something that is out has left, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: patient people put up with a great deal
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet; this letter goes

indicators.note: one who wears clothes is covered by them, so this goes inside

parts.note: lather is the foam from soap
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: An Indian traveller left out of something, and a patient European in foam-soled shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'India's out for long-suffering' means remove the I from the word for long-suffering. The E then sits wrapped in LATHER.
explanation.definitionFit: Patent leather is glossy lacquered hide used chiefly for smart formal footwear such as dress shoes.

clue.text: One may delay service of chicken etc or duck

indicators.note: 'of' marks what follows as the material the answer is made from, its letters lying inside

parts.note: the letters run across the word boundaries

explanation.surface: A restaurant kitchen holding up the serving of poultry dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'service' suggests waiters, but it is a tennis serve; a ball clipping the net cord on a serve is a let and must be replayed.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis the net cord is the cable along the top of the net; a serve clipping it is replayed, delaying play.

clue.text: Capone's done a bunk between one country and another

indicators.note: to do a bunk is British slang for running away, so these letters vanish

parts.note: another country, from which letters are removed
Al Capone, the Chicago gangster; these letters go

explanation.surface: Al Capone fleeing across a border, slipping from one country into another.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the AL from the middle of the other country's name and the first country is left. 'Done a bunk' is British slang for fled.
explanation.definitionFit: Austria is a landlocked nation in central Europe, so it is simply one example of a country.

clue.text: Oddly being ignored, 10 highlighted end of only convenience

indicators.note: skipping the odd-numbered positions leaves just the even ones to keep

parts.note: the answer to 10 across, keeping its second, fourth and sixth letters
something highlighted has been lit up

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone flagging a bit of text about a convenience store, oddly overlooked.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' points to the answer of 10 across, the country; its even letters start the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A utility is something useful or functional, and convenience in the sense of a useful facility shares that meaning of practical usefulness.

clue.text: Part one, so intense, with last two characters having gone west

indicators.text: with last two characters having gone west
indicators.note: west is to the left on a map, so the final pair of letters travels round to the very front

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
deep feelings are intense ones

explanation.surface: A dramatic first instalment of a western, where two characters ride off into the sunset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part one' reads as the opening of a serial, but only 'Part' defines; 'characters' are letters, not people in the story. Across clues read left to right, so 'west' is the start.
explanation.definitionFit: An episode is one instalment or section of a serial, story or series of events, so it is a part of something larger.

clue.text: Vehicle or horse reversing

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a vehicle reversing goes backwards, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: A car or a horse backing up: a choice of transport going into reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vehicle' suggests transport, but here it means a medium of expression, as a newspaper is the organ of a party.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ is a medium for communicating views, such as a party's official newspaper, which is a vehicle for its ideas.

clue.text: Jack's invested in plastic money — ten for satisfaction

indicators.note: to invest is to put funds inside a venture, so one piece goes inside another
plastic can be moulded into any shape, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: Jack puts his credit-card money in, paying a tenner for a bit of pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plastic money' looks like credit cards, but 'plastic' is the anagram signal working on the two words around the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: Enjoyment is the pleasure or gratification taken in something, a close synonym for contentment.

clue.text: Black dog who's come from Germany, perhaps …

parts.note: jet is a deep black stone, hence jet-black
a setter is a breed of gun dog

explanation.surface: A black dog that has arrived from Germany, perhaps a German breed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the definition sound like a dog's pedigree; it is a wealthy traveller just back from a trip abroad, with 'perhaps' marking Germany as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A jet-setter is a rich, fashionable person who flies frequently between foreign destinations, so they may well have just returned from abroad.

clue.text: Twice betray WWII soldier

definitions.meaning: two words each meaning to betray, one after the other: abandon, then inform on
the nickname of the British 7th Armoured Division in North Africa

explanation.surface: A wartime soldier who turned traitor not once but twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' asks for two synonyms of 'betray' joined: one means to abandon your post, the other to squeal. The Desert Rats fought in the North African campaign.
explanation.definitionFit: The Desert Rats were British soldiers of the 7th Armoured Division who fought in the North African desert during the Second World War.

clue.text: … one's ordered 'Hush! Zit!'

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, so the letters are put into a new sequence

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone barking orders at a pimple to be quiet, following on from the black dog in 15 down.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from 15 down, where the dog was mentioned, so 'one' means another dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The shih tzu is a small long-haired toy breed of Tibetan origin, so it is one more kind of dog.

clue.text: Sport in America during which nothing is excessive

indicators.note: what happens during something falls inside its span, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: RU is rugby union
taken as written
US is the abbreviation for the United States
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A sport in the United States where nothing is ever done to excess, or rather where everything is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in America' looks like setting the scene, but 'in' is literal letters followed by US, and the nothing slips between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruinous costs or demands are so extreme they threaten disaster, which matches excessive in the sense of exorbitant.

clue.text: Hundred pound hoard

parts.note: the Roman numeral for a hundred
a pounding head aches or throbs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hundred pound' reads as a sum of money, but 'pound' is the verb for throbbing.
explanation.definitionFit: A cache is a hidden store of goods or valuables, so it is a secret stockpile kept back for later.

clue.text: Ailing from acne?

parts.note: surface reading: suffering from a skin complaint
setter's reading: 'hailing from Hackney' with every H dropped, as a native of East London would say it

explanation.walkthrough: Hackney is a borough in East London; the Cockney accent drops initial H, so 'hailing' becomes 'ailing' and 'Hackney' sounds like 'acne'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner from the East End, known for an accent that drops initial aitches.

clue.text: Act should be cleaner as well as randier occasionally

parts.note: a char, or charwoman, is a cleaner

indicators.note: something done occasionally happens only now and then, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A saucy stage act that ought to be cleaned up, since it is getting raunchier now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: A char is an old British word for a cleaning woman. 'Act' looks like a theatrical turn, but it means a pretence.
explanation.definitionFit: A charade is an absurd pretence put on to deceive, so it is a show or act rather than something genuine.

clue.text: More blasting will require this writer to get into more probing

indicators.note: to get into something is to enter it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: nosier means more inquisitive
the writer speaking of themself

explanation.surface: A quarry engineer saying more blasting will need someone to investigate more deeply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blasting' suggests explosives, but it means loud, as music blasts out.
explanation.definitionFit: Something blasting is very loud, so the comparative form describing greater volume is louder, a synonym of the answer.

clue.text: Bit of a step on, and Master's mounted

indicators.note: in a down clue, mounting means going up, so the letters read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: re means on or concerning, as in letter headings
sir is a title of address for a master

explanation.surface: A Master stepping up onto a mount, part of a step at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' means 'regarding' here, the Latin-derived RE used in memo headings.
explanation.definitionFit: A riser is the vertical board between two treads of a staircase, so it forms one component of each step.

clue.text: Allure shown by French antiheroes

indicators.note: what is shown by something is displayed within it, so the letters are on view inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across the word boundary

explanation.surface: The seductive charm of the brooding antiheroes in French films.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Allure' looks like a noun, but here it is the verb, to attract or charm.
explanation.definitionFit: To allure someone is to attract and charm them powerfully, a close synonym of bewitch or captivate.

clue.text: Pictures found in jumble also by Stubbs originally

parts.note: tat is cheap junk, as at a jumble sale
too means also

indicators.note: the original part of a thing is its beginning, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: Paintings by George Stubbs, the horse painter, turning up among junk at a sale.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumble sale is a British rummage sale, and tat is the cheap stuff sold there. 'Pictures' suggests canvases; these are on skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Tattoos are designs inked permanently into the skin, often images such as anchors or hearts, so they are pictures.

clue.text: Cargo not for return before November period

indicators.note: something sent for return comes back the way it went, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written
November is N in the NATO phonetic alphabet
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A shipment marked not to be sent back before November.
explanation.walkthrough: 'November period' looks like a date, but November is just its phonetic-alphabet letter and the period is a separate word.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonnage is the total weight of goods carried by a ship, so it can stand for the freight or cargo itself.

clue.text: Midwife maybe trains twice around hospital, one that cheers infants up

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for a noun, 'something that cheers infants up'

indicators.note: to go around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: a midwife is one kind of nurse
RY is the abbreviation for railway
the same abbreviation a second time
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs
one, as the speaker refers to themself, is me

explanation.surface: A midwife travelling by train around a hospital, the one who brightens babies' days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twice' asks for the railway abbreviation two times; the second wraps the hospital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Nursery rhymes are short traditional songs and verses sung to small children to amuse and soothe them.
